title: On Pests and Perspectives
content: If you know a weed scientist, you’ll have heard this classic definition: A weed is a plant out of place. The circumstances define the plant. We don’t often consider insects this way, but I started pondering this in my own research system and there are some interesting examples. Earwigs are a pest in some fruits (like cherries) with soft skin that they can chew through, but in apples and pears, they almost never cause fruit damage but can reduce populations of pests like aphids and psyllids. Some of our orchardists are now moving earwigs as a pest control tactic—they are literally transforming the earwigs from a pest into a natural enemy just by changing their location. Another orchard example, the bug Campylomma verbasci, can damage developing apples, but in pear orchards, it is a critical predator of pear psylla. Phytoseiulus persimilis and other predatory mites are typically considered beneficial, except when they are caught noshing on the spider mite Tetranychus lineatus, a classical biocontrol agent of gorse.
